# The Windows I Have Known

The first window I remember was painted shut. It sat at the front of our house on Maple Street, and in early spring I would press my nose to the glass and watch the lilac bush do nothing in particular. The glass was old and slightly wavy, so the street outside always looked as if it were underwater. Cars passed like fish. The mailman swam by every day at ten.

My mother told me the window had been painted shut by the previous owner, a man named Mr. Hedrick who did not trust the world to stay outside. I believed this for years—that windows could be sealed out of spite, or fear, or some private philosophy about what a house owed its occupant. When I finally learned about paint and sashes and the way old houses settle, I was almost disappointed. I liked the idea that a person could decide, in advance, what should be allowed in.

That window gave onto a small front yard and then the road, and beyond the road the Hendersons' maple, which turned the color of a fire deciding to be patient. In October the light came through that tree at a low angle and filled our living room with a copper glow that made even the television look artistic. I did not know then that light is a substance you can be poor in or rich in, that some people live their whole lives in rooms that never get good light, and that this shapes them in ways they cannot name. I thought light was just what happened when you flipped a switch, or didn't.

The kitchen window was a different animal entirely. It looked out onto the driveway and the composter and, past a strip of grass my father mowed in diminishing enthusiasm each August, the fence and the alley. This was my mother's window. She stood at it so much that the linoleum in front of the sink wore a pale crescent, a kind of fossil of her standing. She washed dishes and watched the neighbors and the weather and the birds at the feeder my father filled and the squirrels raided, and she narrated all of it in a low running commentary that was not really addressed to anyone. *There's that cat again. That's the Hendersons' other cat. I don't know whose cat that is.* The window was a screen on which the neighborhood performed, and she was its most devoted critic.

I understand now that she was not watching the cat. She was standing in one of the few places in the house where nobody needed anything from her, and she was looking at a world that did not require her to fix it. The dishes were the price of admission. The window was the point.

My bedroom window faced the back, and at night, if I pulled the shade all the way up and lay with my head at the foot of the bed, I could see a rectangle of sky. In the city you do not get many stars, but I got a few, and the roofline of the garage, and sometimes the moon doing its slow slide behind the telephone wires. I invented constellations because I did not know the real ones. There was one I called the Open Hand, and one I called the Distant Porch, and one that was just a scatter of dim stars I believed was a map of somewhere I would go. I was eight. The window was a prophecy I made up myself.

School windows were for other purposes. They were for watching snow with a desperation that felt almost religious, and for watching rain with a boredom that felt almost geological. They were for locating, on the playground below, the exact position of your best friend, and for noticing, with a pang you had no vocabulary for, the exact position of everyone who was not your best friend. A school window teaches you that life is happening in two places at once—inside the room, where the worksheet is, and outside, where the world is conducting itself with an enticing lack of worksheets. Some people never get over this division. I am one of them. I have built a whole temperament on the suspicion that the interesting thing is happening on the other side of some glass.

My first apartment, at twenty-two, had a window that looked onto an airshaft. This is not entirely accurate. It looked onto a wall two and a half feet away, a wall of weathered brick with a rusted fire escape bolted to it, and if I opened the window and leaned out and craned my neck at an angle that eventually caused a permanent crick, I could see a stripe of sky the color of a mail slot. I lived there two years. I learned, in that room, the essential skill of finding a horizon in a brick. I watched the wall the way my mother had watched the alley. Rain still hit it. Light still crossed it, in a slow migration from upper left to lower right that I used, some mornings, as a clock. A spider took up residence on the fire escape and I followed the architecture of her web the way other people follow the stock market. When a storm tore the web down I felt a grief I did not mention to anyone, and when she rebuilt it overnight I felt a hope of the same size. It was, I later understood, a complete education in how to pay attention, delivered by a window that opened onto almost nothing.

Hospitals have windows, too, and they use them differently. When my father was in the cardiac unit, his room looked out onto a parking structure. The seventh floor of a parking structure is not beautiful. It is a gray floor, a gray ceiling, a low wall, and beyond that the tops of trees, which was the one gesture the view made toward the living world. He was in that room for eleven days. On the third day he noticed the trees. On the fifth day he had opinions about them—which ones were dying, which one was a maple and which was something lesser. On the seventh day he asked me to open the blinds all the way, and then he watched the trees for a long time without talking, and I understood that he was not watching the trees either. He was standing, in whatever way a man in a bed can stand, at the edge of the place where he was needed, and he was looking at a world that, very soon now, was not going to require him to fix it.

I sat in the vinyl chair and watched him watch the trees, and I thought about the kitchen window, the pale crescent worn into the linoleum, and I had to get up and pretend to be interested in the ice machine.

There was a window in the apartment on Delancey Street that I loved for the wrong reasons. It was enormous, nearly floor to ceiling, and it faced west, and in the evening the whole room filled with a light so thick you felt you could pour it. I lived there with someone I thought I would keep. We put a small table by the window and ate dinner in that light as if we were in a photograph of ourselves. I remember the light more clearly than I remember the conversations. I remember the particular amber of a Tuesday in October. I do not remember what we ate. This has always seemed to me an important fact about memory: it keeps the light and loses the plot. The relationship did not survive the following spring, and when I left I stood in the empty room while the movers loaded the truck, and the window did what it always did, which was to fill up with evening, indifferent and generous, and I understood that the light had never been about us. That is the hard, clean lesson of a good window. It will give you everything it has, and it was never yours.

When my friend Ruth died I went to her apartment, because that is what you do, and I sat in her chair and looked out her window, which I had looked out of a hundred times at dinner parties and late conversations, and it looked the same and it looked entirely different. Same fire escape. Same slice of the neighbor's gingko. Same water tower, which she had called, for reasons she never fully explained, the Velvet Antler. The window was still performing the world. It simply no longer had its audience. I sat there for an hour, I think, long enough for the light to change twice, and I understood something that I have been slowly unpacking ever since: that we do not only live in rooms. We live in the views from rooms. We become, in some slow and secret accounting, the sum of the windows we have looked through, and when we die, those windows do not close. They just go on showing the world to whoever is next.

I think about Mr. Hedrick and his painted sash. I think about what he was keeping out. I have looked through a lot of windows since Maple Street, and I have noticed that there are two kinds of looking. There is the looking that scans—cars, weather, the approach of someone you would rather not talk to—and there is the looking that receives. The first kind is a searchlight. The second is a still lake. My mother at the sink had both going at once, the searchlight on the cat and the lake underneath, and maybe that is what a life of attention is: a searchlight with a lake under it.

The window I have now is not the best I have had. It faces a street with a bus stop, a bodega, a tree that the city has planted in a square of dirt too small for it, and the lit sign of a dry cleaner that blinks all night in a way I have stopped minding. In the morning the light comes in low and yellow and lies across the floor like something spilled. I stand at that window with my coffee and I watch a man who walks a dog that walks him, and a woman who runs every day at the same pace, as if she is being reeled in from far away, and the kids from the building across the street who smoke on the steps and laugh at things I will never hear. I know none of their names. I know their coats.

Sometimes I try to add it all up. The painted-shut window, the kitchen crescent, the rectangle of invented stars, the school snow, the brick wall and the spider, the parking structure and the trees my father graded like a disappointed teacher, the Delancey Street amber, the Velvet Antler, this morning light on this ordinary floor. It does not add up to a philosophy. It adds up to a person who has spent a great deal of time at windows, which is to say, a person who has spent a great deal of time at the border between the self and everything else, learning the local weather of that border.

A window is the most honest piece of architecture we have. A door pretends that leaving and arriving are the same thing. A roof pretends the sky is optional. A window makes no such promises. It says: there is a world, and you are not in it, quite, and also you are, because you are looking, and looking is a way of being in a place. It says: you can be warm and it can be snowing. You can be still and it can be moving. You can be alone and it can be full of cats, mailmen, fish, stars, spiders, trees, water towers, buses, and the light that will come tomorrow whether you are there to meet it or not.

I have started, in the last year, to stand at the window at night as well as in the morning. The dry cleaner's sign blinks. Someone is always coming home. The bus sighs at the stop and moves on. And I do what my mother did, what my father did with his parking-structure trees, what I did with the spider and the lilac and the Distant Porch. I look. Not for anything. Just looking. It turns out that was the whole inheritance. Not the houses. Not even the people, exactly, though God knows the people. The looking. The willingness to stand at the glass and receive the world without needing it to be a different world.

The lilac on Maple Street is almost certainly gone. The Hendersons' maple, too. The airshaft wall, the parking structure, the Delancey Street light, Ruth's gingko—all of it scattered, demolished, repainted, re-tenanted, or simply going on without me, which is the same thing from where I stand. But the windows are all still here, in the strange museum the mind keeps, each one still showing its particular weather, its particular hour. I visit them. I put my nose to the glass. The street still looks underwater. The mailman is still swimming by. It is ten o'clock somewhere in 1987, and the light is copper, and my mother is narrating the cat, and I am learning, without knowing it, how to be a person who will one day stand at other windows, in other cities, in other weather, and feel the same thing, which is the feeling of being separate from the world and married to it, at the same time, through a pane of old and slightly wavy glass.
